text:
I’ve found myself thinking about a useful question to ask when somebody shows you a promising new technology: who gets to say, “Hang on, that isn’t right”?

My research team at StoneComms has been looking at solar irrigation, practical AI adoption and digital public infrastructure. An unlikely combination, perhaps, until you think about what happens when one person's decision affects somebody else.

Take solar irrigation. A farmer can have a working pump, a profitable crop and an affordable loan, while drawing from groundwater that neighbours also depend on. Checking the borrower's repayments won't tell you whether the shared water supply is being managed properly. Somebody needs the information — and the authority — to change course.

https://stonecomms.com/research/solar-irrigation-africa-financing-farm-returns-water-limits

The AI paper raises a similar question about information. A tool drawing on government documents needs those documents kept current, conflicts resolved and mistakes recorded. Otherwise, making answers quicker can make outdated information travel further. Paying for a fast answer isn't much of a saving if someone then has to undo a bad decision. Who can challenge the answer, and does that challenge improve the next one?

https://stonecomms.com/research/practical-ai-adoption-sub-saharan-africa-procurement-local-adaptation-productivity

That becomes especially consequential when public systems connect identity, payments and other services. Imagine an incorrect record being reused across several agencies. The connections intended to save you repeating your details could also save the system repeating its checks. The promise is faster, less costly public service. But how do you get a mistake corrected everywhere — and access the service while you're waiting?

https://stonecomms.com/research/digital-public-infrastructure-africa-procurement-interoperability-accountable-service-delivery

What interests me is that the ability to correct a system deserves as much attention as the ability to expand it. I'd like to hear more project pitches that explain what happens when someone objects, a record is wrong or conditions change.

Coming up, the team is sharing existing research on another deceptively simple question: how can Ethiopia turn renewable generating capacity into dependable power for factories and households? We're also looking at the work needed to turn national climate plans into infrastructure projects that can actually be financed and held accountable.

I thought you might enjoy these papers. As always, they're free to read, and you can follow my team here:
https://www.linkedin.com/company/stonecomms/

If you're working through a similar question about African infrastructure, investment or public services, do get in touch. I always enjoy hearing what people are working on.

#AfricanInfrastructure #DigitalPublicInfrastructure #ResponsibleAI #ClimateInvestment
